IJGB diaries: How selfish are we? — Part 1

Dianne_-_
Oct 11, 2026

Originally written: Jan 4, 2025

This is for the IJGBs*. This is for the IJGBs who spent most of the first two decades of their lives in Nigeria and now only come home on special occasions.

We complain when things change: when the garlic sauce in shawarma is replaced with mayonnaise (one of Nigeria’s biggest atrocities btw), when the flavour of Milo is so mild that you need to put half a tin in for the same kick a tablespoon would have given you ten years ago, when the Coke bottle repeatedly says “Less Sugar, Great Taste!” as if Coke is trying to convince us that the nasty aspartame they’ve snuck into the bottle can make up for the fact that we are paying the same price for a subpar version of the drink.

Never mind that our complaints are justified because they are legitimate things to complain about, but are they dignified?

We left. We left Nigeria with the option to come back as visitors with higher dispensable cash and even though we left and have been gone for a long time, we expect that things would remain the same for us, just for us, just how we liked it. We left but we live with the mindset that we can have the best of both worlds: the cushy comfort of the ‘abroads’ and the rugged familiarity of home whenever we return.

We can run back to the cold, dreary UK and face their lackluster version of Fanta Orange as long as we know the real deal awaits us back home. If the Fanta at home is replaced with the same dishwater liquid version the UK endures, we become irate. But at whom? And why? Do we expect the wheels in a country we no longer serve to continue to turn for us and keep things as they were to remain to our taste? What about the people who didn’t leave, who couldn’t? What if they want some semblance of the kind of lives we have in the ‘abroads?’ even if it’s a counterfeit version of it? Even if half the food trucks at the park don’t have food in their trucks and there’s an endless variety of knock-off, flavour-drained chocolate drinks?

Should we ever complain? I guess the first question to ask is “Are we doing anything to keep the quality of Nigeria up?

If our answer is ‘no,’ then we need to get comfortable with replacing the love we once had for a love we should now have. If our answer is ‘yes,’ then we need more people to say ‘yes,’ because our contributions clearly aren't enough to make the dent we need to keep Nigeria together.

I write this in reflection of my own thoughts whenever I go home, and how I’m quickly reminded that it’s selfish to yearn for the old Nigeria when I’m no longer truly in it, part of it, or contributing to it in a way that can sustain what it once was (yet). But should the IJGBs even want it to be as it was? Where the only fast food options were Mr. Biggs, Tantalizers or the Mama Put that our parents warned us against? Or should we be happy now that there is more variety despite it being at the expense of our childhood favourites?

Should the comfort of a nostalgia that we can re-live whenever we go home outweigh the progression of a country for those who are still truly in it?

(There’s another conversation to have here about how this ‘progression’ — especially the boom in variety — can only be enjoyed by the Nigerian elite because we all know that the average Nigerian is poor).

*IJGB — I Just Got Back: A term used to describe Nigerians who live outside Nigeria, especially in the UK or the US, and have returned for holidays. Particularly those who grew up in Nigeria before moving abroad.
